bib.title: Learn to Explain: Multimodal Reasoning Via Thought Chains for Science Question Answering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Learn to Explain: Multimodal Reasoning via Thought Chains for Science Question Answering". Lu, Mishra, Xia, Qiu, Chang, Zhu, Tafjord, Clark, Kalyan. NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv 2209.09513v2).

COVERAGE: All 22 pages, 80,013 of 80,013 chars, including the checklist and appendices A and B. I skimmed the references. Page numbers below come from the printed page footers.

CLAIMS
1. Dataset size and composition. There are 21,208 multiple-choice questions, split 60:20:20 into 12,726 / 4,241 / 4,241. Context mix: image 10,332 (48.7%), text 10,220 (48.2%), both 6,532 (30.8%), none 7,188 (33.9%). As exclusive bins: image only 3,800 (17.92%), text only 3,688 (17.39%). Images are diagrams ≈7,372 (34.8%) or natural photos ≈2,960 (14.0%). 52.08% of questions have only 2 options.
   quote: "Out of the 21,208 questions in SCIENCE QA, 10,332 (48.7%) have an image context, 10,220 (48.2%) have a text context, and 6,532 (30.8%) have both." (p4, Table 1, Fig 3b)
2. Headline accuracy, test set (Table 3). Human 88.40, GPT-3 CoT (2-shot, QCM→ALE, text-davinci-002) 75.17, UnifiedQA-base fine-tuned 70.12 and 74.11 with CoT, best VQA model VisualBERT 61.87, random 39.83.
   quote: "if we prompt GPT-3 with chain-of-thought prompting (QCM→ALE), we obtain the state-of-the-art result so far (75.17%)." (p7). On image questions: "a 20.07% gap for questions with the image context (IMG) between humans and our best performing model" (p8).
3. Models that get a caption instead of the image beat the models that see it. This is the shortcut signal; the paper never frames it that way. UnifiedQA and GPT-3 never see pixels: "the image is converted into a caption" (p6), made by a ViT+GPT-2 captioner with "maximum length of generated captions is 16" (p18). Zero-shot GPT-3 with captions already scores 74.04 overall and 65.74 on IMG. VisualBERT, which receives the actual image, scores 61.87 overall and 62.17 on IMG.
   quote: "Without any fine-tuning, GPT-3 already reaches almost the best performance we can get." (p7)
4. Blind and no-image baselines, an ablation of Top-Down (Table 3, p8):
   - Q only 39.85, CI only 39.87. Both near random, but neither sees the answer options.
   - Q+M (no context) 54.44. Q+CT+M (text context, no image) 56.61. Q+CI+M 58.26. Full QCM 59.02.
   - Adding the image to Q+M is worth about 3.8 points. The authors read this as robustness.
   quote: "The results achieved in blind studies of Q only and CI only are close to random chance, showing that the SCIENCE QA dataset is robust and reliable in distribution." (p9). Also: "all input components provide critical information" (p9).
5. Generating lecture and explanation gives small gains. Feeding in the gold explanation gives large ones.
   - Gains from generating them: +1.20 for GPT-3 and +3.99 for UnifiedQA.
   - Gold explanation in the input: 94.13 (QCMLE*→A) against 75.17. This is a leak of the answer's reasoning, so treat it as an upper bound only.
   - Explanation before answer hurts: QCM→LEA 55.4 against QCM→ALE 73.6, on 1,000 test examples.
   - UnifiedQA with CoT matches no-CoT accuracy using 40% of the training data.
   quote: "QCMLE*→A outperforms QCM→ALE by 18.96%" (p9). Table 7: "QCM→LEA Random 55.4 ... QCM→ALE Random 73.6" (p10)
6. Explanation quality. 65.2% of GPT-3 CoT explanations were rated "gold" (relevant, correct and complete) by majority vote of 3 MTurk workers. UnifiedQA CoT scores best on BLEU and ROUGE but only 56.9% gold.
   quote: "65.2% of explanations meet the gold standard of human evaluations" (p2, Table 4 p9)

LIMITS
- The authors concede that captions are weak: "these captions lack fine-grained semantics and usually do not work well for diagrams" (p20, B.4). Diagrams are 34.8% of the data.
- There is no blind baseline for the strong models. No GPT-3 or UnifiedQA run drops the caption on image questions, so the paper cannot say how many IMG questions are answerable without the image. The only no-image ablation uses the weak Top-Down model.
- The "robust" claim rests on Q-only and CI-only runs that lack the options. That makes near-random expected, so it is not evidence against shortcuts.
- The GPT-3 results come from a single in-context trial (trial ID 1). Error bars exist only for Fig 7, from 4 repeats.
- The test split is random, not held out by skill. The data comes from IXL under CC BY-NC-SA, non-commercial only. The human baseline is MTurk workers at $6/hr, not domain experts.
- Dated: text-davinci-002, UnifiedQA-base and 2022 VQA models.

BUILDS ON
- Chain-of-thought prompting: Wei et al., arXiv 2022 [54].
- Explanations generated after the answer: WT5, Narang et al., arXiv 2020 [41].
- UnifiedQA: Khashabi et al., Findings of EMNLP 2020 [19].
- GPT-3 few-shot: Brown et al., NeurIPS 2020 [4]. The paper's text cites [5] for GPT-3, but [5] is Chen et al., a citation error in the paper.
- Top-Down attention: Anderson et al., CVPR 2018 [1].
- VQA: Antol et al., 2015 [2].
- Making the V in VQA matter: Goyal et al., CVPR 2017 [11]. It is cited only as a VQA dataset, not for its shortcut finding.

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Best candidate: Table 3 (p8), "Evaluation of baselines over different classes in accuracy (%)". One table shows the no-image ablations, captions-only LLMs beating image-seeing VQA models, and the human gap.
- Alternative: Fig 3b (p4), "Question distribution with different context formats". A pie chart of the image / text / both / none mix.

PROBLEMS
- The text in Fig 1 and Figs 4, 15, 16 and 17 is font-garbled in the extraction (Caesar-shifted glyphs). I relied only on their captions and surrounding prose.
- Internal inconsistency: the share with an explanation is 90.5% in Table 1 but "91.3%" on p4.
- No embedded instructions.
